issues.item: Humiliation: I feel permanently humiliated by what happened
issues.explanation: For a life-threatening illness trauma, 'permanently humiliated' is hard to reconcile unless the illness involved a specifically shaming interpersonal circumstance; nothing else in the profile suggests that context. The other items center danger, fear, vivid reliving, and generalized threat, so humiliation stands out as clinically mismatched to the trauma type.

vignette: Emmett's life had always been about control and precision. As a database administrator, he took pride in keeping complex systems running smoothly, and his meticulous nature served him well in his work. But all of that changed two years ago when he was diagnosed with a life-threatening illness. The months that followed were a blur of hospital visits, surgeries, and endless tests. It started with the smell of disinfectant. Even now, whenever Emmett catches a whiff of it, he's transported back to those sterile hospital corridors. He can feel the beeping of machines, the antiseptic taste in his mouth, and the crushing sense of vulnerability that came with being at the mercy of his own body. The memories are more real to him than anything else – more vivid than his wedding day, more alive than the birth of his children. Emmett's lost count of how many times he's relived those moments since then. It happens without warning: he'll be working on a project, or watching TV, and suddenly he's back in that hospital bed, feeling like he's suffocating under the weight of his own mortality. His body tenses up, his heart racing as if it's happening all over again. He's tried to explain it to himself – intellectually, he knows he's safe now – but his body won't listen. It keeps reacting as if danger is still lurking around every corner. He's constantly on guard, even in the comfort of his own home. The silence makes him jumpy; every creak of the floorboards sounds like a threat. Emmett used to think he was a rational person, but now he's consumed by negative emotions – fear, anger, guilt, shame. He feels like he's lost faith in everything: people, life, even God. The world seems like a treacherous place, full of hidden dangers waiting to pounce. His work has suffered as a result. Simple tasks take him twice as long, and his colleagues have started to notice the change. They try to be understanding, but Emmett can sense their frustration. He's withdrawn from social events, unable to bear the thought of being around others who don't understand what he's going through. His divorce hadn't helped – his ex-wife had been supportive during the illness, but afterwards, they'd grown apart. Emmett felt like a burden to her, and she seemed to feel suffocated by his new anxieties. Now, he lives alone in a house that feels too big, too empty. It's been two years since the diagnosis, and Emmett's finally realized that he can't keep living like this. The hypervigilance is exhausting; he can barely sleep anymore. He's started to wonder if he'll ever be able to shake off this sense of perpetual danger. That's what brought him to therapy – a desperate hope that someone might be able to help him find his way back to the man he used to be. As he sits in the waiting room, fidgeting with his hands, Emmett can't help but wonder: will anyone ever understand what it's like to live in this constant state of fear? Or am I doomed to spend the rest of my life trapped in this never-ending nightmare?
